Jordan — really appreciate the usage sample, that helps a lot. High level answers below, then a suggested commercial path.

Batching & KV cache:
- Continuous batching will reduce per-token compute by aggregating concurrent requests — for your 600 QPS bursts we should see 20–40% token-cost reduction versus naïve single-request serving, depending on seq-length mix.
- KV/prefix caching helps if many users share similar prompts or system messages (e.g., same assistant instructions). With ~70% prefix reuse across the cohort we often see an extra 15–25% net token cost saving because KV cache avoids recomputing earlier layers.

Quantization tradeoffs:
- INT8 / 4-bit (QLoRA-style) can cut model memory and improve throughput on compatible runtimes. Expect minor quality deltas on few-shot tasks; for instruction-following generative tasks, plan an eval set and an A/B rollout.
- For the cohort experiment I recommend starting with conservative 8-bit quant for the canary variant, then a controlled switch to 4-bit on segments where quality delta < 1.5% per your evals.

Commercial suggestion (short experiment):
- 6-week cohort packet: 6 weeks of usage credits (applied as dollar credits) sized to your expected token consumption + a 12% cohort-discount on top of list for the committed tranche.
- If you want a deeper discount in exchange for a pilot commit, we can structure a 3-band commit: 50k / 200k / 500k tokens (or equivalent $ commit).

Next steps:
1) Can you confirm average prompt / completion token lengths in the sample?
2) If you’re OK with the commercial path above, I’ll loop in Grace (pricing) and Laura (deploy/ops) for an ops & legal-ready term sheet.

- Karthik
Director, Sales Engineering — Redwood Inference
